content: The phylogenetic and epidemiologic evidence suggests that human rabies can have an incubation period spanning multiple years. This finding underscores the complexity of rabies pathogenesis and the need for long-term vigilance in exposed individuals. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published technical reports, such as the 2018 WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies, which provide comprehensive guidelines for rabies prevention and control. These reports emphasize the importance of mass dog vaccination campaigns, public education, and intersectoral collaboration to eliminate rabies at its source. The natural history of rabies, as detailed in foundational texts, highlights the progression of the disease in both humans and animals. Rabies is almost universally fatal once clinical symptoms appear, making prevention through vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) critical. Studies conducted in various regions, such as Haiti and Cambodia, have examined community knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding rabies risk. These studies reveal gaps in awareness and the need for targeted educational interventions to improve rabies prevention and management. Research in Kazakhstan and other endemic regions has documented the burden of rabies and the challenges in controlling its spread. Surveillance programs and novel approaches, such as canine rabies burden estimation in Haiti, have been implemented to better understand and address the disease. Intersectoral programs, such as the Bohol Rabies Prevention and Elimination Project in the Philippines, demonstrate the effectiveness of coordinated efforts to eliminate both human and canine rabies. These programs integrate vaccination, public education, and community engagement. Rabies surveillance in the United States and other countries has provided valuable data on the epidemiology of the disease, including trends in animal reservoirs and human exposures. This information is critical for guiding public health interventions. The safety and immunogenicity of various rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin regimens have been extensively studied. For example, the 2-1-1 intramuscular post-exposure rabies vaccine regimen has been shown to be effective in severely exposed patients. Cost-effective strategies for rabies control, such as the use of intradermal vaccination schedules and reduced-dose rabies immunoglobulin administration, have been explored to improve accessibility and sustainability in resource-limited settings. Educational programs aimed at preventing dog bites and rabies exposure, particularly among children, have been shown to be effective in reducing the incidence of injuries and subsequent rabies risk. Mass dog vaccination campaigns remain the cornerstone of rabies control efforts. Achieving at least 70% vaccination coverage is essential to establish herd immunity and interrupt rabies transmission in dog populations. The One Health approach, which integrates human, animal, and environmental health, is critical for the successful implementation of rabies control programs. This approach fosters collaboration among veterinary services, public health agencies, and community stakeholders. Dog population management, including the humane handling and vaccination of free-roaming dogs, is a key component of rabies control strategies. Studies of dog ecology and ownership practices help inform the design and implementation of effective vaccination campaigns. Rabies control programs must be flexible and responsive to changes in epidemiological conditions. Routine evaluation of vaccination coverage and community engagement are essential to ensure the success and sustainability of these programs. Cross-border collaboration and international cooperation are vital for the elimination of rabies, particularly in regions where the disease remains endemic. Strengthening surveillance and diagnostic capacity, as well as ensuring the availability of high-quality vaccines, are critical components of these efforts.
